1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: This patient was a 58-year-old man engaged in farming at home. He was first hospitalized on Day 0, and hospitalized for the second time on Day +401. At the first hospitalization, his chief complaint was chest tightness and shortness of breath for 20 days. Twenty days earlier, after catching a cold, he developed chest tightness and shortness of breath, accompanied by cough and sputum production, with a small amount of white mucoid sputum, without hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, chest pain, palpitations, or precordial discomfort. He was treated at a local clinic for "upper respiratory tract infection" with anti-infective therapy, expectorant therapy, and other symptomatic supportive treatment (details unknown), but without obvious effect. He then presented to the emergency department of our hospital, where chest CT showed bilateral interstitial lung changes with infection. He was given intravenous drip of "etimicin 0.3 g once daily and bromhexine 8 mg once daily," after which his symptoms improved slightly, and he was admitted through our outpatient department with a diagnosis of "interstitial lung disease." Since onset, the patient's appetite and rest were fairly good, bowel and bladder habits were normal, and body weight had no obvious change. The patient had previously been healthy. He had smoked for 30 years, averaging 20 cigarettes/day, and denied a family history of malignancy. Physical examination at that time showed: T 36.5 ℃, P 89 beats/min, R 20 breaths/min, BP 101/76 mmHg. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes was palpable throughout the body. On auscultation, breath sounds were coarse in both lungs, with no dry or wet rales heard. Chest CT on Day -9 showed multiple round air-containing lucencies in both lungs; bronchial dilatation in both lungs, more prominent in the left upper lobe, with a curly hair-like appearance; nodular high-density opacities in the right middle and lower lobes, the largest located in the right lower lobe, approximately 1 cm in diameter; and multiple patchy high-density opacities in both lungs with indistinct borders, more prominent in the left upper lobe. The preliminary diagnosis at that time was interstitial lung disease. Ancillary examinations showed: ESR 24 mm/h; CBC, CRP, procalcitonin, coagulation, endotoxin, fungal D-glucan, galactomannan peptide, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, cardiac enzymes, and electrolytes were all normal; Mycobacterium tuberculosis antibody was positive, while Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA, TB infection T-lymphocyte test, and PPD test were negative; autoantibodies, ANCA, and rheumatologic panel were negative; tumor markers NSE 16.98 ng/ml and SCC-Ag 2.7 ng/ml; arterial blood gas analysis (FiO2 21.0%) showed pH 7.417, pO2 70.9 mmHg, pCO2 38.5 mmHg, and SaO2 92.4%. PFT suggested mild obstructive ventilatory dysfunction (FEV1/FVC 65.47%, FEV1/pred 87.7%). Bronchoscopy was performed on Day +3. Endoscopic findings showed: bilateral bronchi were patent, with no obvious mass or stenosis; abundant white viscous secretions were seen on the left side; mild hyperemia was seen in the lingular segment of the left lung; and no obvious hyperemia or edema was seen in the remaining lumens. BALF sent for bacteriologic and pathologic examinations was negative. After admission, the patient was treated with levofloxacin combined with etimicin for anti-infective therapy. Repeat chest CT on Day +6 showed no obvious change compared with Day -9. The patient reported symptomatic improvement after anti-inflammatory treatment and was discharged on Day +6 with the diagnosis of "COPD, secondary pulmonary interstitial changes." Chest CT on Day +248 showed emphysema, multiple pulmonary bullae in both lungs, bilateral interstitial pulmonary inflammation with infection (more prominent in the left upper lobe), and nodules in the right middle and lower lobes. This follow-up indicated worsening of the left upper lobe lesion compared with before. We recommended rehospitalization for repeat bronchoscopy, but the patient declined inpatient treatment because his symptoms had not worsened. On Day +401, one year after the previous hospitalization, he returned to our hospital again with the chief complaint of "chest tightness and shortness of breath for more than 1 year, worsening for 1 week." Chest CT on Day +400 showed bilateral interstitial lung changes with inflammation in the right middle and upper lobes and the left lung, increased compared with before (Day +248); emphysema with bullae formation; nodules in the right middle lobe and both lower lobes, without significant change compared with the previous film; and left pleural thickening. Comparison of the above chest CT scans suggested that the area of consolidation in the left upper lobe had enlarged and had a honeycomb-like appearance, and ground-glass opacity and a small amount of honeycombing had appeared in the left lower lobe.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis (predominantly smear-negative/bacteriologically negative, chronic fibrocavitary, or bronchogenic disseminated tuberculosis)
supporting_evidence: The patient is a 58-year-old man engaged in farming at home, with chest tightness, shortness of breath, cough, and expectoration of white sputum; the course has lasted for more than 1 year and is accompanied by radiographic progression, consistent with the characteristics of chronic pulmonary infectious disease.
TB antibody positive

Chest CT suggested that the left upper lobe lesion persisted and gradually worsened; the area of consolidation in the left upper lobe had enlarged and was honeycomb-like. There were multiple patchy high-density opacities in both lungs with indistinct borders, most prominent in the left upper lobe, consistent with upper lobe-predominant chronic destructive changes.
Chest CT on Day +400 showed left pleural thickening, which can be seen in chronic tuberculous pleural/pulmonary parenchymal disease with scarring.
After anti-infective treatment, repeat chest CT on Day +6 showed no significant change compared with Day -9, suggesting a poor response to conventional antibacterial therapy
The image shows peripheral consolidation in the left upper lung with multiple air-containing lucencies/honeycomb-like changes, with imaging features of a chronic destructive lesion.
opposing_evidence: No typical tuberculous constitutional symptoms such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss
Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA, tuberculosis infection T-lymphocyte assay, and PPD test were negative
Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid obtained by bronchoscopy was sent for bacteriologic and pathologic examinations; both were negative.

On bronchoscopy, no obvious mass or stenosis was seen; only a relatively large amount of white viscous secretions on the left side and mild congestion of the lingula of the left lung were observed, with no more direct bronchoscopic evidence of TB.

differential_diagnoses.name: Nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease (NTM pulmonary disease)
supporting_evidence: A protracted disease course, slow radiographic progression, and limited response to conventional anti-infective therapy, consistent with the common clinical course of nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease

Chest CT showed bronchial dilatation in both lungs, more prominent in the left upper lobe, accompanied by multiple patchy opacities and progressively worsening structural destruction of the left upper lung, suggesting the possibility of mycobacteria-associated bronchiectasis with chronic infection.

Chest CT on Day +400 showed increased inflammation in the right middle and upper lobes and the left lung compared with previously; ground-glass opacities and a small amount of honeycombing appeared in the left lower lobe, suggesting a chronic airway-disseminated/multifocal process
Bronchoscopy revealed more abundant white, thick secretions on the left side, suggesting a background of chronic airway infection.
Imaging shows a focal chronic destructive lesion in the left upper lung with bronchiectatic changes.
opposing_evidence: The first-stage information did not provide definitive evidence of a positive mycobacterial culture or acid-fast stain.
Negative TB-related tests do not support TB, but they are also not direct evidence of NTM

The patient's chief complaints were mainly chest tightness and shortness of breath, with a small amount of sputum, and there was a lack of the more typical history of long-term sputum production seen in NTM pulmonary disease.

differential_diagnoses.name: Chronic fungal lung disease/chronic pulmonary aspergillosis
supporting_evidence: The patient has underlying emphysema, pulmonary bullae, bronchiectasis, and chronic structural lung disease, all of which are common predisposing backgrounds for chronic pulmonary aspergillosis.

There is persistently progressive focal consolidation in the left upper lobe, accompanied by multiple air-containing lucencies/honeycomb-like destruction, consistent with the appearance of chronic destructive lesions seen in chronic fungal infection.
No significant imaging changes after standard antibacterial therapy, suggesting the possibility of a non-common bacterial infection.
The left upper lung lesion on the image shows a peripheral distribution with multiple internal air-cavity-like changes, and should be differentiated from a chronic fungal destructive lesion.
opposing_evidence: Fungal D-glucan and galactomannan peptide were normal
Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid obtained by bronchoscopy was sent for bacteriologic and pathologic examinations; both were negative.
The patient had no fever, and the first-stage information did not describe common manifestations of chronic aspergillosis such as hemoptysis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Smoking-related interstitial lung disease/idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (with emphysema, CPFE or UIP-like changes)
supporting_evidence: The patient has smoked for 30 years, averaging 20 cigarettes/day, which is an important risk factor for smoking-related parenchymal lung disease.
Multiple chest CT scans showed interstitial changes in both lungs and emphysema with pulmonary bullae formation
Chest CT on Day +400 showed ground-glass opacity and a small amount of honeycombing in the left lower lobe, possibly consistent with fibrotic changes within the interstitial lung disease spectrum.

Arterial blood gas analysis showed mild hypoxemia (pO2 70.9 mmHg, SaO2 92.4%), and PFT indicated mild obstructive ventilatory dysfunction, which can be seen in interstitial lesions with concomitant emphysema.

Autoantibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and the rheumatologic panel were negative, making connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease relatively unsupported; idiopathic or smoking-related types should be considered
opposing_evidence: The lesions are predominantly characterized by focal consolidation and honeycomb-like destruction in the upper lungs, especially the left upper lobe; the distribution is atypical and does not completely conform to the classic UIP pattern of lower-lobe and subpleural predominance.
Associated bronchiectasis, patchy opacities, and inflammatory changes are more suggestive of an infectious or other focal process.

In the first-stage information, symptom onset was associated with “catching a chill” and was accompanied by cough and sputum production; this is not a typical mode of onset for isolated interstitial lung disease.

differential_diagnoses.name: Lung adenocarcinoma (pneumonic-type/invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma) or other pulmonary malignancy with secondary post-obstructive changes
supporting_evidence: The patient is a 58-year-old man with a long-term smoking history and is at high risk for lung cancer.

Chest CT showed nodular hyperdense opacities in the right middle and lower lobes, with the largest measuring approximately 1 cm; in 2019, nodules were still present in the right middle lobe and both lower lobes, suggesting consideration of multiple nodular tumors or accompanying lesions.

The left upper lobe area of consolidation has gradually enlarged, with no significant radiographic change after anti-infective therapy; vigilance is needed for a pneumonia-like tumor or tumor-related fibrosis/necrotic changes.
Left pleural thickening may be seen in neoplastic or chronic inflammatory lesions adjacent to the pleura
opposing_evidence: Bronchoscopy showed patent bilateral bronchi, with no obvious mass or stenosis.
Pathologic examination of BALF was negative
Tumor markers showed only NSE 16.98 ng/ml and SCC-Ag 2.7 ng/ml; the phase 1 information did not provide stronger evidence of malignancy.
The imaging shows multiple air-containing lucent areas within the lesion, honeycomb-like changes, and bronchiectasis, more suggestive of chronic infection or a fibrodestructive lesion.

differential_diagnoses.name: Organizing pneumonia (cryptogenic or secondary)/nonresolving bacterial pneumonia
supporting_evidence: There was a history of exposure to cold before onset, followed by chest tightness, shortness of breath, cough, and sputum production, with a background of post-infectious or post-inflammatory pulmonary consolidation.

Chest CT showed multiple patchy high-density opacities in both lungs with ill-defined borders, more pronounced in the left upper lobe; in 2019, ground-glass opacity was again seen in the left lower lobe, consistent with the consolidation and ground-glass opacity seen in organizing pneumonia
The patient reported slight symptomatic improvement after anti-inflammatory treatment, suggesting that inflammatory lesions cannot be completely excluded.
opposing_evidence: Complete blood count, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin were all normal, not supporting active common bacterial infection
After anti-infective treatment, repeat chest CT on Day +6 showed no significant change compared with Day -9, with poor radiographic resolution.

The lesion has persisted over a long period and developed honeycomb-like/structurally destructive changes, which is not the typical evolution of simple organizing pneumonia or common bacterial pneumonia.
Bacteriologic and pathologic examinations of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid obtained by bronchoscopy were both negative

stage2_input.text: After the patient's second admission, lung tumor markers showed that SCC-Ag had increased to 5.5 ng/ml compared with previously (2.7 ng/ml at the first admission). Arterial blood gas analysis (FiO2 21%): pH 7.475, pO2 45.9 mmHg, pCO2 34.5 mmHg, SaO2 81.6%. Pulmonary function testing indicated moderate to severe obstructive ventilatory dysfunction (FEV/FVC 57.51%, FEV1/pred 52.8%). Arterial blood gas analysis was consistent with type I respiratory failure, and the patient's condition had worsened significantly compared with one year earlier.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Chest CT suggests that lung cancer cannot be excluded
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 58-year-old male long-term smoker with recurrent and persistent chest tightness and shortness of breath for more than 1 year, with marked worsening over the past 1 week. Multiple prior CT scans showed continued progression of a left upper lobe lesion, with no significant long-term resolution after anti-infective treatment, and the development of honeycomb-like and cystic changes as well as ground-glass opacity in the left lower lobe, suggesting that simple infection or a nonspecific interstitial process cannot explain the entire course. The purpose of repeat chest CT is to further determine whether the lesion is showing neoplastic progression, assess the extent of left upper lobe consolidation, changes in bilateral pulmonary nodules and suspected disseminated lesions in the left lower lobe, and analyze whether there are signs of bronchiolar obstruction, pleural involvement, and complications, thereby providing imaging evidence for whether histologic confirmation is necessary, selection of the biopsy site, and subsequent staging assessment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Respiratory failure is a contraindication to bronchoscopy.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although bronchoscopy 1 year ago did not reveal any obvious endobronchial mass or stenosis, and BAL bacteriology and pathology were also negative, imaging has since shown continued progression, and chest CT has already indicated that lung cancer cannot be excluded. Prior negative results alone cannot rule out a peripheral malignant lesion or a malignancy with spread along the airways. Reconsidering bronchoscopy is intended to allow direct visualization of the airway while also obtaining further specimens, thereby providing a route to a definitive diagnosis; however, the patient currently has type I respiratory failure, and bronchoscopy itself may precipitate or worsen hypoxemia, so proposing this examination first is also to assess its indications and contraindications, and then decide whether to perform it after blood gases improve. The clinical value of this examination lies in addressing the core question of "whether diagnostic evidence can be safely obtained via the airway route."

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Following discussion with the patient's family, bronchoscopy-guided transbronchial lung cryobiopsy was performed. On Day +403, bronchoscopy-guided transbronchial lung cryobiopsy was performed, and the specimen was satisfactory.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has a long disease course with लगातार progressive radiographic worsening. The left upper lobe lesion has progressively enlarged with honeycomb-like/cystic changes. Prior anti-infective treatment was ineffective, and conventional bronchoscopy did not reveal an endobronchial mass, suggesting that lavage or brush cytology alone might be insufficient to establish the diagnosis. At this point, choosing transbronchial cryobiopsy under bronchoscopy was, under the premise that chest CT was highly suspicious for malignancy and histologic evidence had to be obtained, intended to improve sampling depth, tissue volume, and diagnostic yield by directly obtaining a more satisfactory specimen from the progressive lesion, in order to distinguish invasive adenocarcinoma from chronic infection, organizing lesions, or interstitial lesions. This examination is निर्णायक for the final definitive diagnosis and subsequent pathologic subtyping and molecular testing; however, because the patient has underlying respiratory failure, it should also be performed cautiously after improvement in blood gases, with strict precautions against risks such as pneumothorax and bleeding.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Biopsy pathology report: invasive adenocarcinoma of the "left native upper lobe"
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Although the patient had a long-term smoking history, lesion progression, and imaging findings suggesting possible lung cancer, there had previously been long-standing infectious and interstitial changes, and bronchoscopy and BAL had yielded negative results; therefore, a definitive diagnosis still could not be established clinically on the basis of symptoms, CT, and elevated tumor markers alone. The core purpose of pathologic biopsy is to directly determine the nature of the lesion and answer the key question: "Is it a malignant tumor, or a chronic infection/organizing lesion/other interstitial lesion?" After obtaining pathologic evidence, not only can the diagnosis of lung cancer be confirmed, but the histologic type can also be clarified, providing the basis for subsequent immunohistochemistry, molecular classification, clinical staging, and selection of the treatment plan; this is the most critical link in the diagnostic pathway in this case.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Immunohistochemistry: TTF-1 (+), Napsin A (+), p53 scattered (+), p16 (+), TS (+), EGFR (+), p40 (-), Ki-67 (+) 20%, PD-1 (-), PD-L1 (-).
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: After the pathologic biopsy suggested invasive adenocarcinoma, further confirmation of the tumor origin and direction of differentiation is still required by immunohistochemistry. The patient's imaging manifestations are complex, including a primary lesion in the left upper lobe, multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules, and a ground-glass opacity in the left lower lobe, requiring differentiation as to whether these represent primary pulmonary adenocarcinoma and its dissemination. Positivity for TTF-1 and Napsin A and negativity for P40 help support primary pulmonary adenocarcinoma rather than squamous cell carcinoma or tumors of other origins. Ki-67 can reflect proliferative activity, while markers such as PD-L1 are related to the assessment of subsequent systemic treatment options. Therefore, this examination not only serves pathologic subtyping after confirmation of the diagnosis, but also directly affects exclusion in the differential diagnosis and determination of the subsequent treatment pathway.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Genetic testing showed a BRAF V600 mutation; EGFR, ALK, ROS1, MET, BRAF, and HER-2 were all negative.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has already been definitively diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma by biopsy pathology and immunohistochemistry. The next most important clinical question is whether there are driver gene alterations that can guide targeted or individualized therapy. Because the lesions in this case have shown obvious progression, and intrapulmonary metastasis in the left lower lobe is being considered, this patient belongs to the group requiring treatment decisions as soon as possible. Genetic testing can further define the molecular subtype and screen for driver events such as EGFR, ALK, ROS1, MET, HER-2, and BRAF. Detection of a BRAF V600 mutation has direct value for determining the tumor's biological characteristics, assessing the possibility of targeted therapy, and discussing prognosis and treatment options with the family; therefore, this test is a key step in moving from 'pathologic confirmation' to 'precision treatment decision-making.'

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Chest CT indicated that lung cancer could not be excluded. To establish the diagnosis, a biopsy was required. Respiratory failure is a contraindication to bronchoscopy. After anti-inflammatory, bronchodilator, and expectorant treatment, arterial blood gas analysis was repeated while on oxygen, with PaO2＞60mmHg. Considering that bronchoscopy 1 year earlier showed a patent airway lumen with no mass or stenosis, after discussion with the patient's family, transbronchial cryobiopsy was performed. On Day +403, transbronchial cryobiopsy was performed, and the specimen obtained was satisfactory. After the biopsy, the patient's shortness of breath worsened markedly. ECG monitoring indicated that pulse oxygen saturation dropped to 60%. Pneumothorax after cryobiopsy was considered. On physical examination, percussion of the left lung was tympanitic, and breath sounds over the left lung were absent on auscultation. Closed thoracic drainage was immediately performed on the left side, and the patient's symptoms gradually improved. The biopsy pathology report showed invasive adenocarcinoma in the "left native upper lobe." Immunohistochemistry: TTF-1(+), NaspinA(+), P53 scattered(+), P16(+), TS(+), EGFR(+), P40(-), Ki67(+)20%, PD1(-), PD-L1(-). Genetic testing showed a BRAF V600 mutation; EGFR, ALK, ROS1, MET, BRAF, and HER-2 were all negative.

They were unwilling to continue systemic evaluation and were also unwilling to pursue further treatment, and chose self-discharge.
